songs.title: Grieg: In the Hall of the Mountain King
songs.downloaded: Grieg - In the Hall of the Mountain King.mp3
songs.arc_from_web: Opening (first ~15%): sneaking low bassoons and pizzicato basses tiptoe through the theme over a horn pedal, dark and mischievous, as Peer creeps into the cave. Early middle (~15-45%): the theme repeats and rises in register, passing to strings and woodwinds, with tension coiling as more trolls gather. Middle (~45-75%): the brass and full orchestra join, with a steady crescendo and accelerando turning the creeping into a stomping chase. Climax (~75-95%): a wild, very fast frenzy with cymbals and timpani crashes, the trolls in full pursuit. Ending (last ~5%): sudden hammer-blow chords and an abrupt cut-off, as if the mountain hall collapses.
songs.research_recording_note: Peer Gynt Suite No. 1, the orchestral version (not a piano or rock arrangement): Herbert von Karajan with the Berlin Philharmonic (Deutsche Grammophon). It is easy to find, and its very soft opening and blazing, very fast close give the widest swing in loudness and density, which is the most useful range for judging widgets. The incidental-music version with chorus (for example Neeme Jarvi with the Gothenburg Symphony) is a richer alternative.

songs.title: Saint-Saëns: Danse Macabre
songs.arc_from_web: Opening (about the first 5%): a harp strikes twelve over hushed strings while midnight falls. Then Death tunes his fiddle on a jarring tritone, and the eerie solo violin calls the dead from their graves. First third: a sly waltz begins in the flute and strings, and the xylophone joins with rattling bones. The mood is spooky and playful at once. Middle (about 35-65%): the dance spreads through the whole orchestra. A distorted Dies irae appears as a mocking, grotesque chorale, and fugal passages swirl. Final third: everything builds to a wild, frenzied climax with full brass and pounding percussion. Last 10%: an oboe rooster crows at dawn and the frenzy collapses. The violin plays a last wistful phrase, and the skeletons slip back into their graves on soft pizzicato.
songs.research_recording_note: Get the orchestral version, not Liszt's piano transcription. The orchestral score has the textures this piece is known for: the detuned solo violin, the xylophone bones, the harp striking midnight and the oboe rooster. Charles Dutoit with the Philharmonia Orchestra (Decca) is widely available. Yannick Nézet-Séguin with the Philadelphia Orchestra is a good modern alternative. Both have a strong solo violin and clear percussion.

songs.title: Holst: Mars, the Bringer of War
songs.arc_from_web: The first fifth opens quietly: col legno strings, harp and timpani tap a 5/4 rhythm, and bassoons and horns add a low, creeping theme, so the menace builds from far off. Through the next stretch the ostinato swells while the brass grows louder, and it builds to the first huge, dissonant brass climax, like an army arriving. In the middle the meter turns toward a heavier, dragging march: tenor tuba and trumpet fanfares sound over the drums and the ostinato machinery, and tension stays high with only short moments of slack. Around the final third the opening rhythm comes back fully armoured: the whole orchestra hammers it out in unison, there is a crushing build-up with the organ, and it reaches the most dissonant pile-up of the piece. It ends with brutal, grinding chords, held pauses and final hammer blows on a single note, an exhausting, mechanical end with no triumph.
songs.research_recording_note: Use the full orchestral version, not a piano arrangement, because the col legno strings, the snare, the brass and the organ pedal make up its texture. The Montreal Symphony Orchestra under Charles Dutoit (Decca, 1986) is widely available and has powerful, clear sound with strong low brass. Herbert von Karajan with the Berlin Philharmonic (DG, 1981) is a good alternative.

songs.title: Barber: Adagio for Strings
songs.arc_from_web: Opening (first ~third): the violins play a long, hushed melody that moves stepwise, like a chant. It rests on sustained chords and feels suspended and grieving. Middle (~third to two-thirds): the theme passes to the violas and then the cellos. The parts pile up and each ascent climbs higher, so the tension grows like rising waves of pain. Climax (~70-75%): all the strings strain upward into a high, brittle, almost unbearable fortissimo outcry. It is cut off by a long, shocking silence. Aftermath (last ~quarter): soft, hymn-like chords return. The opening melody comes back, quiet and spent. It ends unresolved, fading on an open chord, like acceptance or a held breath.
songs.research_recording_note: Leonard Bernstein with the New York Philharmonic (Sony, 1971), or his slower 1980s Los Angeles Philharmonic recording on DG. Choose the orchestral string version, not the original quartet movement or the Agnus Dei choral arrangement. The full string section gives the layered, dense texture that builds to the climax. Both recordings are easy to find.

songs.title: Stravinsky: Firebird, Berceuse and Finale
songs.note: This download holds ONLY the Berceuse and the Finale, not the Infernal Dance: the arc below covers three movements, use its last two thirds.
songs.arc_from_web: The Infernal Dance (about the first third) opens with a single violent orchestral blow, then becomes a jagged, syncopated frenzy. Brass stabs, a pounding timpani and xylophone, and a whirling ostinato drive it as Kastchei's monsters are forced to dance to exhaustion, ending in a crash. The Berceuse (the middle third) drops suddenly into stillness: a slinky, hypnotic bassoon lullaby floats over shimmering harp and muted strings, dark and tender, with oboe answers. It sinks into a long, frozen, near-silent string tremolo, the spell of sleep. The Finale (the last third) starts out of that hush with a solo horn singing a simple folk-like hymn, quiet like dawn. The melody passes through the strings and grows in a long crescendo to full orchestra, then is recast in broad, stamping 7/4 brass chords for a blazing, triumphant ending of rebirth.
songs.research_recording_note: Choose an orchestral recording of the 1919 suite, not a piano version, because the orchestration is the main draw. Two good options: the Philharmonia conducted by Esa-Pekka Salonen, or the San Francisco Symphony conducted by Michael Tilson Thomas. Both are widely available and well recorded, and have strong brass and a clear bassoon solo. If you want the music Disney used in Fantasia 2000, that is the Philharmonia under James Levine.

songs.title: Mussorgsky: Night on Bald Mountain
songs.arc_from_web: Opening (first ~10%): whirling strings and blaring brass, as unearthly voices and spirits gather on the mountain at midnight. First third: Chernabog appears in heavy, menacing brass and is glorified. Middle (~30-75%): the witches' sabbath and black mass build into a wild, swirling, ever more frenzied dance, with repeated climaxes and shrieking winds. Turn (~75-80%): a distant village church bell rings out and the spirits scatter as the frenzy collapses. Final fifth: a calm daybreak, with a solo clarinet and flute over soft strings and harp, fading into peace.
songs.research_recording_note: Rimsky-Korsakov orchestral version, not Mussorgsky's rawer 1867 original or Stokowski's Fantasia arrangement. A good recording to download is Claudio Abbado with the London Symphony Orchestra or Berlin Philharmonic, which is widely available. Georg Solti with the Chicago Symphony Orchestra is another option. These recordings were picked from general knowledge, not from the search. The Rimsky arrangement is the famous one. Its storm, dance and quiet bell-and-dawn ending give the strongest dramatic contrast for the widget compositions.

songs.title: Liszt: Hungarian Rhapsody No. 2 (orchestra version)
songs.downloaded: Franz Liszt - Hungarian Rhapsody No.2 (Orchestra version).mp3
songs.note: The user downloaded the ORCHESTRAL version, not the piano original.
songs.arc_from_web: The opening (lassan, first ~third) is dark and declamatory: heavy C-sharp minor octaves and proud, brooding recitative-like phrases, like a gypsy bandleader's solemn introduction, broken by ornate flourishes and imitations of the cimbalom. A playful, lilting transition follows, with a sly dance theme in F-sharp major, hinting that the mood is about to turn. The friska (from roughly 40%) starts light and skittish, with staccato repeated notes and a glittering high register. It keeps speeding up and thickening into stomping csardas rhythms and hand-crossing fireworks. Near the end (last ~10%) comes a pause for an optional cadenza, then a breathless prestissimo that whirls to a triumphant, crashing close.
songs.research_recording_note: The original solo piano version is the best choice for texture work: it has bare octaves, cimbalom-like tremolos and sudden virtuoso runs. Download Marc-André Hamelin's recording (Hyperion), which includes his own cadenza, or Georges Cziffra's (EMI/Warner) if you want the most wild, improvisatory reading. For a lusher orchestral alternative, use the Liszt/Doppler orchestration in Herbert von Karajan's recording with the Berlin Philharmonic (DG).

songs.title: Satie: Gymnopédie No. 1 (Monochrome Jazzy Mix)
songs.note: The user added this as an extra. It is a jazzy remix (Monochrome Jazzy Mix), not the plain Satie piano piece. Keywords: melancholy and ennui (Wikipedia, Entrada masterclass), dusk light and soft mist (French notes), Sunday afternoon and empty rooms (weaker blogs); slow dance, drifting stillness and smoky late-night are inferences from the title and the arrangement.

songs.title: Tchaikovsky: Romeo and Juliet, Fantasy-Overture (20:25, cut by Claude into six song packs at quiet points)
songs.arc_from_web: Opening (first ~20%): a hushed, archaic clarinet-and-bassoon chorale for Friar Lawrence, with dark string murmurs and harp, building foreboding. Next (~20-35%): the feud bursts in, a furious allegro of syncopated strings and cymbal crashes like clashing swords. Then (~35-50%): the love theme rises on English horn and violas, a sighing muted-string answer, then a lush full-string climax of nocturnal longing. Middle (~50-75%): development and recapitulation where strife and the Friar's theme collide, the love theme returning even more ecstatic before being cut down by the feud. Final (~75-100%): a timpani-driven funeral march, the love theme broken and mournful in the strings, a quiet chorale of consolation, then hammered closing chords.
songs.research_recording_note: Full orchestral (1880 final version): Claudio Abbado, Boston Symphony Orchestra (DG) or Valery Gergiev, Mariinsky/Vienna Phil. Orchestral rather than piano, because the texture (woodwind chorale, string tremolo, cymbal 'sword' clashes, English horn/viola love theme) is the point for widget testing. Abbado/Boston is widely available and well balanced.

pieces.what: 1. Friar Laurence (introduction: the chorale, harp, the slow build to a first climax)
2. The feud (allegro giusto: syncopated strings, cymbal sword-clashes), then a hushed transition
3. Love theme (English horn and violas, the muted-string sighs, the full-string climax, the balcony night)
4. Clash (development: feud against the Friar chorale, to a loud climax)
5. Return and catastrophe (recapitulation: the feud returns, the love theme ecstatic, then cut down)
6. Coda (timpani funeral march, the love theme broken, the consoling chorale, the hammered last chords)

songs.note: Section names are Claude's reading of the loudness curve and the usual form; the analyst must confirm them by ear-analysis.
